judge: Claude Code subagent, Claude Opus 5.5, fresh

items.label: A
items.critique: Three rumour lines that each point at the wider plot (the dead waking, mages banned, where the inn is); plain exclamations and a direction, exactly the campaign's town chatter.

items.label: B
items.critique: The tall tale of fending off 40 wizards bare-handed and the child proud of a brother running the trial have the campaign's broad, cheerful humour and short sentences.

items.label: C
items.critique: Ogre-neighbourhood joke and 'good luck to ya' are Nox-like, but the three lines form a neat comic arc about one subject, which feels composed for the slot.

items.label: D
items.critique: 'The old goat' gossip about a master taking an apprentice and the dismissed skeleton rumour are dry, character-first and lightly ironic, as Westwood's townsfolk are.

items.label: E
items.critique: Two of three lines restate the same spider-in-the-mayor's-house beat, the comic aside about the mayor's fear is explained, and the typo ('off you back') reads planted.

items.label: F
items.critique: Quest-hook townsfolk who name the stolen item, the thieves and the player's role, with a missing period; more briefing than gossip.

items.label: G
items.critique: 'Breakdowns in the city' and a 'Chief Engineer' who can't keep track are out of Nox's register, and the news line copies a stock Westwood frame.

items.label: H
items.critique: Panicked siege lines with a cynical closer ('Let them take it, I say'); short, plain, the campaign's crowd under threat.

items.label: I
items.critique: The aside that the villainess 'has style' and 'only fools and warriors' are staying is Westwood's dry, slightly cheeky crowd voice.

items.label: J
items.critique: Bandits on trade routes and brazen ogres on caravans are generic travel warnings; the 'strange noises' from alleys is vague filler rather than a Nox rumour with a hook.

tells: Westwood's townsfolk each say one different thing, usually about the larger plot or a named character, with a quick character opinion; new texts tend to make all three lines circle one local quest (spiders, scepter, ogres) and repeat its facts.
New texts lean on generic fantasy-travel warnings (trade routes, caravans, strange noises) and occasionally out-of-world nouns (engineer, breakdowns).
Westwood's humour comes as a flat, unexplained opinion ('the old goat', 'has style'); new texts explain or set up the joke.
Reused Westwood frames ('If you want the latest news, go to...') in a new town are a sign of imitation.
